title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 271 (Circumstances in which company may be wound up by Tribunal)

content.overview: Section 271 provides that a company may be wound up by the Tribunal if (a) the company has, by special resolution, resolved that it be wound up by the Tribunal; (b) the company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality; (c) on an application under s. 224 made by the Registrar or any person authorised by the Central Government, the Tribunal is of opinion that the affairs of the company have been conducted in a fraudulent manner or the company was formed for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or the persons concerned in formation or management have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or misconduct; (d) the company has made a default in filing its financial statements or annual returns for immediately preceding five consecutive financial years; or (e) the Tribunal is of opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up. Inability to pay debts as a free-standing Companies Act ground is not the current debt-default route; that is under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
content.glance: Tribunal may wind up on: special resolution; acts against sovereignty/security/public order etc.; fraud (s. 224 path); 5 consecutive years' filing default; just and equitable. Debt default → IBC, not this section as primary route.
content.study: A company may be wound up by the Tribunal on the grounds listed in section 271. Current-law framing: map facts to one of the five limbs; note that inability to pay debts is addressed under the IBC rather than as a free-standing Companies Act ground; who may petition is s. 272; just and equitable is not ordered on bare loss of confidence alone. Chapter XIX sick-company provisions are omitted.

sections.heading: Special Resolution
sections.body: Company by special resolution resolves that it be wound up by the Tribunal.

sections.heading: Sovereignty and Related Grounds
sections.body: Company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality.

sections.heading: Fraud
sections.body: On application under s. 224 by Registrar or CG-authorised person: affairs conducted fraudulently, or company formed for fraudulent/unlawful purpose, or persons concerned guilty of fraud, misfeasance or misconduct.

sections.heading: Filing Default
sections.body: Default in filing financial statements or annual returns for immediately preceding five consecutive financial years.

sections.heading: Just and Equitable
sections.body: Tribunal of opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up.

provisions.title: Circumstances in which company may be wound up by Tribunal

examples.title: Five-year filing default
examples.body: A company has not filed financial statements or annual returns for five consecutive financial years. That default is a ground for Tribunal winding up under s. 271.

examples.title: Debt default not this route
examples.body: A creditor seeks to wind up solely for unpaid debt. The primary current route for debt default is the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, not a free-standing inability-to-pay ground under s. 271.

hypotheticals.question: Is bare loss of confidence enough for just and equitable winding up?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Just and equitable winding up requires facts that justify the remedy (e.g. breakdown of quasi-partnership substratum or similar). Bare loss of confidence is not enough.

distinctions.left: Special resolution, sovereignty, fraud, 5-year filing default, just and equitable
distinctions.right: Corporate insolvency resolution and liquidation for debt default under IBC

misconceptions.trap: Any unpaid creditor can petition under s. 271 for inability to pay debts as under the old company law.
misconceptions.correction: Inability to pay debts is not the free-standing current Companies Act route. Debt default is primarily under the IBC. Section 271 lists specific grounds including special resolution, fraud, five-year filing default and just and equitable.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 271 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Map facts to a listed ground. II. Exclude bare debt-default as Act route. III. Link petition under s. 272. IV. Conclude.

Just and equitable is not bare loss of confidence.
